messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Thomas

Thomas was thirty-two when the convoy hit the IED outside Kandahar. He remembers the noise first—not the explosion itself, which his mind seems to have erased, but the ringing that came after, a high-pitched whine that filled everything. He remembers the smell of burning rubber and something else, something organic that he has never been able to name. He was the vehicle commander. Martinez and Dawson were in the Humvee behind his. When the dust cleared enough to see, both vehicles were burning. He pulled three men from his own truck. He could hear Martinez calling out, but the second vehicle was already fully engulfed. Thomas tried twice to reach it. The heat drove him back. He has spent twenty-eight years knowing that he left them there.

The guilt settled into him like scar tissue. It was not the sharp, fresh guilt of the first months—that had been almost easier, because it had felt like something he deserved. What came later was worse: the slow, corrosive certainty that he had survived when better men had not, that there was something fundamentally wrong with the fact of his breathing while they were ash. He came home, married Carol ten years later, kept working. For a long time, he had almost convinced himself he could live with it. But in the past few years, something had shifted. The guilt had metastasized into a broader, darker conviction: that he did not know who he was anymore, that the man who came back from Kandahar was not the person he had been before, and that the world itself was a place where death could come without warning and take the people you cared about. He had come to believe that nowhere was truly safe—that vigilance was the only honest stance toward a fundamentally dangerous existence.

These convictions had begun to shape what he did and did not allow himself to experience. When memories of the event surfaced—and they did, unbidden, when he was loading pallets in the warehouse or sitting in traffic—they came with an intensity that terrified him. The terror was not abstract. It was the same physical sensation he had felt in the moment: his chest tight, his vision narrowing, his hands shaking. Accompanying the terror was a crushing weight of guilt that made him want to disappear. The memories were also strangely wordless. He knew what had happened, he could see it, but when he tried to articulate it—even in his own mind—the words scattered like startled birds. There was no language adequate to what he had done or failed to do.

Because these memories were unbearable, Thomas had begun to construct a careful architecture of avoidance. He stopped wearing the tan cargo pants he had worn in the service; they triggered something in him that he could not quite articulate, a sense of being pulled back into that identity, that failure. He had not returned to the military base where he had been stationed, though it was only two hours from his home. The thought of driving past those gates, of seeing the landscape where he had trained, made his chest tight with dread. More insidiously, he had begun to avoid thinking about the event at all, pushing away any memory or association the moment it arose. He would change the radio station, leave a room, find a task that demanded his full attention. Carol had noticed that he became irritable when she tried to talk about his service, and he had stopped attending the veteran support group he had gone to for a few months.

But the avoidance was not protecting him. Instead, it was feeding the very beliefs that had taken root in him. Each time he turned away from a memory, each time he refused to let himself think about what had happened, he was implicitly confirming his deepest fear: that the truth was too dangerous to face, that the guilt was too heavy to bear, that he was fundamentally unsafe in his own mind. The more he avoided, the more he felt like a stranger to himself—a man made of evasions and suppressions, no longer sure what was real or solid in his own experience. And the more distant he became from his own past, the more the world seemed to close in. He found himself scanning parking lots before he got out of the car. He slept poorly, alert to sounds. He could not relax with Carol the way he used to. His conviction that the world was dangerous felt less like a belief and more like a simple fact, confirmed every time he successfully avoided something that might hurt him. The avoidance had become a way of life, and the life it was creating was smaller and more isolated with each passing month.

At sixty, Thomas finally called a therapist. Carol had given him an ultimatum: get help, or she was leaving. He had sat in the parking lot for fifteen minutes before going in, terrified that talking about Kandahar would break something in him that could not be repaired. What he wanted most was to feel like himself again, to know who that person was. What he feared most was that there was no going back—that the guilt and the terror and the wordlessness were all that remained.
